title: The Fifteen-Hundredth Term
statement: Let $a_1 < a_2 < a_3 < \dots$ be all the positive integers whose base-$2$ representation, written without leading zeros, has strictly more digits equal to $1$ than digits equal to $0$. Find the remainder when $a_{1500}$ is divided by $1000$.
hints: Group the terms of the sequence by their number of binary digits. Write a number as a leading $1$ followed by $d$ free digits, and work out how many $1$s those $d$ digits must contain.

The $d$ free digits must contain $j$ ones with $2j \ge d$. Counting these strings is a sum over the upper half of row $d$ of Pascal's triangle, so use the symmetry of binomial coefficients to evaluate it. Once the length of $a_{1500}$ is known, find its digits from left to right by counting how many valid numbers have a $0$ in each position.

The half-row sums show that $1199$ terms have at most $11$ digits, so $a_{1500}$ is the term of rank $301$ among the $12$-digit terms. These are the numbers whose last $11$ digits contain at least $6$ ones. At each position, with $m$ digits after it and $r$ ones still needed, a $0$ leaves $\sum_{j \ge r} \binom{m}{j}$ completions. If the current rank is at most this count, the digit is $0$. Otherwise the digit is $1$, and you subtract the count from the rank and reduce $r$ by $1$. Run this procedure through all $11$ positions and convert the resulting binary string.
solution: Take a number with $d + 1$ binary digits. It is a leading $1$ followed by $d$ free digits. If $j$ of the free digits are $1$, the number has $j + 1$ ones and $d - j$ zeros, so it is a term exactly when $j + 1 > d - j$, that is, when $2j \ge d$. Hence the number of terms with $d + 1$ digits is $$T_d = \sum_{2j \ge d} \binom{d}{j}.$$ Since $\binom{d}{j} = \binom{d}{d-j}$, this sum is half of row $d$ when $d$ is odd, so $T_d = 2^{d-1}$. When $d$ is even, the central term is counted in the sum and has no partner, so $T_d = \frac{2^d + \binom{d}{d/2}}{2}$. For $d = 0, 1, \dots, 10$ this gives $$1, 1, 3, 4, 11, 16, 42, 64, 163, 256, 638,$$ which add up to $1199$. Also $T_{11} = 2^{10} = 1024$ and $1199 + 1024 = 2223 \ge 1500$. So $a_{1500}$ has $12$ digits, and it has rank $1500 - 1199 = 301$ among the $12$-digit terms. These are the numbers whose last $11$ digits contain at least $6$ ones. Let $N(m, r) = \sum_{j \ge r} \binom{m}{j}$ be the number of binary strings of length $m$ with at least $r$ ones. Among numbers of equal length, those with a $0$ at the first position where they differ come first. Suppose the current rank is $R$, that $r$ more ones are needed, and that $m$ digits follow the current position. A $0$ here leaves $N(m, r)$ completions. So if $R \le N(m, r)$ the digit is $0$ and nothing changes. If $R > N(m, r)$ the digit is $1$, $R$ is replaced by $R - N(m, r)$, and $r$ is replaced by $\max(r - 1, 0)$. Starting from $R = 301$ and $r = 6$: $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{position after the leading } 1 & m & r & N(m,r) & R & \text{digit} \\ \hline 1 & 10 & 6 & 386 & 301 & 0 \\ 2 & 9 & 6 & 130 & 301 & 1 \\ 3 & 8 & 5 & 93 & 171 & 1 \\ 4 & 7 & 4 & 64 & 78 & 1 \\ 5 & 6 & 3 & 42 & 14 & 0 \\ 6 & 5 & 3 & 16 & 14 & 0 \\ 7 & 4 & 3 & 5 & 14 & 1 \\ 8 & 3 & 2 & 4 & 9 & 1 \\ 9 & 2 & 1 & 3 & 5 & 1 \\ 10 & 1 & 0 & 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 11 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \end{array}$$ Therefore $a_{1500}$ has binary representation $101110011101$, so $$a_{1500} = 2048 + 512 + 256 + 128 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 2973.$$ The remainder when $a_{1500}$ is divided by $1000$ is $973$. Why this works. binomial-selection, base-representation: once the leading $1$ is fixed, the condition depends only on how many of the free binary digits are $1$, so binomial counts give both the length of the term and each of its digits.
